turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Nuala. Come on in and sit yourself down. This is your routine review, but I can see you've something on your mind.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I have, doctor. I've been awful anxious. I stopped the cholesterol tablet after I read a thing online, and I haven't slept right since.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been turning it over and over. I'm Sinead, I come in weekday mornings to help with the tablets and the breakfast.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand to meet you, Sinead. Nuala, which cholesterol tablet was it, and what dose?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. Twenty milligram. The little white one.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): And are you still taking it, or have you stopped altogether?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped it in March. Or the end of February, I can't rightly say. I'd been on it for ages, and then I left it off after that article.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): So twenty milligram, stopped around February or March, after being on it a good while. Not a tablet you only tried the once.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it. Is that dangerous? Will my arteries clog up in a month? I read that statins wreck your muscles.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll not jump to that. Any muscle pain, aches, or weakness?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No aches. I'm grand that way.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. And the blood pressure tablet, the ramipril, are you taking that every morning?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): The chemist on the main street was shut for the bank holiday, so I went over to the one beside the church. They hadn't my usual box.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you about the chemist. I'm asking about the ramipril itself. Are you taking it every day?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, every other day. I thought five milligram every day was a lot, so I spaced it out.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's worse than every other day some weeks. I'm only there mornings, and Tuesday and Thursday are still in the blister pack when I come back.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the dose is five milligram, meant for every morning, but you take it every other day, and Sinead thinks more get missed. How long have you had the high blood pressure?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Five-ish years. Maybe longer. I wouldn't swear to the year. Is five milligram too strong? Should I be on two point five?
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five milligram is a modest dose. I wouldn't drop it over a worry. Five-ish years is what I'll record. Any chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): And shortness of breath?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I can get up the stairs. A bit slower, but I'm not gasping.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Dizziness?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. I do get light-headed if I stand up quick, but it passes.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Light-headed on standing. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of months, maybe. Is that the pressure dropping too low, even though I skip days?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can happen with ramipril, and skipping days can also let the pressure bounce up. Any cough?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): The high cholesterol, was that found around the same time?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Around then, yes. They said it was high. Six point something. I can't remember the decimal. Does that mean I'm in danger this week?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): We won't use a half-remembered number. I'll repeat the bloods. Tell me about the thing you watched online.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): A video, yer man saying statins cause muscle damage and you should come off them. Am I going to seize up? Should I be in hospital?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not from what I'm hearing. You said you'd no aches. Calves, thighs, shoulders, still grand?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, my calves have been sore. I didn't think it counted. It's not terrible.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sore calves. How long, and what brings it on?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, I'd say. Worse on the stairs. Grand when I'm sitting down with a cup of tea.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's longer than a fortnight. She was complaining before I went on leave, and that was three weeks ago at least.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Was it? I thought a fortnight. I don't know now. Does that mean the statin is still in me? I stopped it months ago.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): A statin stopped in the spring wouldn't still be in the muscle. We'll say the calf pain is roughly two to three weeks, worse on the stairs, eased by sitting. Any true weakness, or dark urine?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness where I can't stand. The urine is the normal colour. Why, is dark urine bad?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can signal severe muscle breakdown. You're not describing that. Let me take the blood pressure while you're sitting quietly.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's one hundred and forty-eight over ninety-two. Pulse is seventy-six, nice and regular.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one hundred and forty-eight high? My neighbour said anything over one-twenty is a stroke waiting. Will I have a stroke this week?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): One hundred and forty-eight over ninety-two is above where I'd like it, not an emergency. I think it's sitting up because the ramipril isn't going in every day.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She had a home reading last week she said was one-sixty over something. She didn't write it down.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): A number that isn't written down I can't use. We'll stick with today. Ankles aren't swollen. Heart sounds are steady. Chest is clear.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not in heart failure? My uncle was. Is that in the family? My father had a heart attack in his seventies.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): No signs of heart failure today. I'll note your father had a heart attack in his seventies. An uncle I won't hang a label on. Do you smoke?

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked. My husband did, years back. He has diabetes. His pills are metformin, a thousand milligram, on the same counter as mine. I get terrified I'll take his by mistake.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you ever actually taken his metformin?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I never took them. I just stare at the boxes. Should they be in a different press? What if I take one in the night when I'm half asleep?
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I moved his box to the top shelf last week. She hasn't touched it.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep them apart, top shelf is fine. You haven't diabetes yourself in our notes. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. The dentist gave me penicillin last year and I was grand.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): No known drug allergies, then. What about alcohol?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): A small glass of wine on a Sunday, not every Sunday. Is wine bad with the ramipril? And are eggs full of cholesterol, because I read that too?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): A small glass is neither here nor there. Eggs in moderation won't decide this. I'm more concerned with the tablets. Let me say it back so we're sure.

[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ramipril five milligram, meant every morning, taken every other day, and some doses may be missed. Atorvastatin twenty milligram stopped around February or March. Calves sore for roughly two to three weeks, worse on stairs. Light-headed on standing for a couple of months. No chest pain, no cough, no gasping. Pressure today one hundred and forty-eight over ninety-two, pulse seventy-six.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): That's fair. I'm still not sleeping, though. Awake half the night worrying. Would a sleeping tablet be all right, or is that dangerous with the ramipril?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): I have the poor sleep from the worry. I'm not adding a sleeping tablet today. It isn't a dangerous mix in itself, but it isn't what you need this week.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Are you putting me back on the statin now? What if the video was right? What if my liver is damaged already?

[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not restarting the atorvastatin today. There's no story today of severe muscle breakdown. We'll repeat fasting bloods, the cholesterol and the liver tests, and the kidney bloods because of the ramipril, and then decide.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting from midnight? Can I have water? Will it be the big needle? I hate the big needle.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Water is fine. No food from midnight. It's an ordinary needle. I'll put the form in for this week.
[SEG0065] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can bring her Thursday morning. She'll fret if we leave the day vague.
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thursday morning is perfect. Then I want you back here in a month. We'll look at the results together and decide about the statin then. Not before.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): A whole month? What if the calves get worse, or I get proper chest pain? Do I sit and wait?

[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): You don't wait for those. If the calves turn to real weakness, or the urine goes dark, or you get chest pain or breathlessness, ring the surgery the same day. If it's severe, go to the emergency department.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): And the ramipril, do I go back to every day from tonight? What if I go light-headed and fall?

[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Five milligram every morning, from tonight, not every other day. If you feel properly faint, sit or lie down and ring us. Don't take your husband's metformin under any circumstances.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the salt? My husband's nurse told him to cut the bread. I mostly did the same. Is brown bread all right?

[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): Brown bread is fine. Keeping the salt down is worth doing, but the daily ramipril matters more than the bread. You never smoked, a little wine, carer in on weekday mornings. I have the picture.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): She isn't here at weekends. Who checks the pack on Saturday? I forget when I'm on my own.
[SEG0074] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can leave the Saturday and Sunday tablets in a separate cup on the Friday. That worked before.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do that. If the mid-week pack is still full, Sinead, ring the surgery and let us know the doses aren't going in.
[SEG0076] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will. I'll mark the card.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): And the blood test, do I take the ramipril the morning of the test or skip it? I don't want to do the wrong thing.
[SEG0078] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take it as normal that morning, with water. Just no food. The kidney bloods are fine with the tablet on board.

[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So Thursday for the bloods, ramipril every morning, his metformin on the top shelf, and back to you in a month about the statin. Did I miss anything that could kill me?

[SEG0080] person_1 (DOCTOR): You've got it. Nothing you've told me says you're about to come to harm this week. The pressure is up, the statin is paused, and we'll decide that properly when the bloods are back.
[SEG0081] person_2 (PATIENT): If the cholesterol is sky high, will you force the statin back on me? Can I say no?
[SEG0082] person_1 (DOCTOR): You can always say no. I'll explain the numbers, and we'll choose together. I won't be forcing a tablet down you.
[SEG0083] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Thanks, doctor. I feel a small bit less like I'm about to keel over. Not completely. But a small bit.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Weekend tablets on Friday is supported; ringing surgery if mid-week pack full is directed to caregiver, not patient.
bad.text: Set weekend tablets out on Friday and ring the surgery if the mid-week pack is still full (action_type=other, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Atorvastatin 20 mg had been taken for ages before being stopped around February/March; it was not a one-off trial.

Ramipril 5 mg was prescribed/meant to be taken every morning, but the patient has been spacing it to every other day and the caregiver reports some weeks Tuesday and Thursday doses are still left in the blister pack.
The patient denied muscle pain/aches/weakness initially when specifically asked about possible statin side effects.
Shortness of breath denial included that she can get up the stairs, only a bit slower, and is not gasping.
The patient reported high cholesterol had previously been 'six point something' but could not remember the decimal.
No known drug allergies was specifically documented, supported by tolerating penicillin from the dentist last year.
Pulse was not only 76 bpm but specifically described as nice and regular while measured.
Doctor assessment: no signs of heart failure today.
Family history is incomplete/wrongly recorded: the father had a heart attack in his seventies, not just an unspecified heart attack.
The patient does not have diabetes in the notes, and she has never actually taken her husband's metformin despite worrying she might by mistake.
Doctor stated they are not adding a sleeping tablet today; poor sleep is thought to be from worry and a sleeping tablet is not what is needed this week.
Plan nuance missing: atorvastatin is specifically not being restarted today, and the decision about restarting will wait until after the blood results are reviewed together.
Planned investigations also include repeating kidney bloods because of ramipril and repeating fasting bloods this week with the form put in by the doctor.
The doctor advised the patient to restart ramipril 5 mg every morning from tonight.
The caregiver specifically agreed to leave Saturday and Sunday tablets in a separate cup on Friday because the patient forgets when alone at weekends.

There was a real shared decision-making statement: even if cholesterol is very high, the patient can refuse the statin and the doctor will explain the numbers and choose together rather than force treatment.
